p.x:
Last summer, my family went to Krabi. The beach was beautiful, with white sand and blue water. My little brother looked for shells, and I found a small crab under a rock.
In the afternoon, we took a boat trip. The water was very deep and clear. Suddenly, my dad shouted, "Look! Dolphins!" Five dolphins were swimming next to the boat. It was amazing! The guide said there are no sharks near this beach, and whales sometimes visit in winter.
Then we went snorkelling. Under the water, I saw colourful coral, a turtle eating seaweed and an octopus hiding in the rocks. We had to be careful because there were some jellyfish. In the evening, we sat on the shore and watched the sunset. It was the best day of the holiday.

p.t: Learning to Dive in Koh Tao
p.x:
Koh Tao, a small island in the Gulf of Thailand, is one of the most popular places in the world to learn scuba diving. Every year, thousands of people come here to do their first diving course.
A beginner's course usually takes three or four days. First, students learn the theory and practise in a swimming pool. Then they make four dives in the sea. The maximum depth for beginners is 18 metres. Instructors teach them how to check their equipment, how to breathe slowly and what to do if there is a strong current.
The reefs around Koh Tao are full of marine life. Divers often see colourful fish, turtles and sometimes even a whale shark, the largest fish in the sea. However, the reefs are in danger. Boats, sun cream and rubbish pollute the water, and old fishing nets get stuck on the coral. Some dive schools now organise clean-up dives to collect rubbish from the seabed and from the harbour.
One instructor said, "When people see how beautiful it is underwater, they want to protect it."

The ocean covers more than 70 per cent of the Earth's surface and produces about half of the oxygen we breathe, much of it from tiny plankton. Yet this vast aquatic world is under threat as never before.
Overfishing is one of the most serious problems. Industrial trawlers drag enormous nets along the seabed, catching everything in their path and destroying habitats that took centuries to form. Scientists estimate that over a third of fish populations are now exploited beyond sustainable levels.
Climate change adds further pressure. As the ocean absorbs carbon dioxide, it becomes more acidic. This acidification makes it harder for creatures such as crabs and shellfish to build their shells. Warmer water, meanwhile, causes coral bleaching, in which corals lose the algae that give them colour and food. Large areas of reefs, home to a quarter of all marine species, have already died.
Pollution, too, reaches every corner of the sea. Microplastics have been found not only along the coast and in shallow waters but even in the abyss, thousands of metres below the surface, where submarines have discovered plastic bags on the ocean floor.
There are signs of hope, however. Where governments have established protected areas, fish numbers and biodiversity have often recovered within a few years. The tide, it seems, can still be turned, if action is taken quickly.
